newsitem.title: USA: NHL ice hockey - NO MORE JOKES ABOUT THE MIGHTY DUCKS OF ANAHEIM.
newsitem.headline: NHL ice hockey - NO MORE JOKES ABOUT THE MIGHTY DUCKS OF ANAHEIM.

text.p: Four years ago, the idea of a Disney-owned team named "The Mighty Ducks" joining the National Hockey League was laughed at by ice hockey purists across North America.
No one is laughing now that the team is in the second round of the playoffs.
No more snickering about the team's macho drake mascot "Wild Wing" rappeling down a rope to a rink called "The Pond".
No more guffaws at children filling seats wearing Donald Duck-like goalie masks and greeting the team with choruses of quacks from wooden duck-calls.

The Mighty Ducks of Anaheim, whose name was based on a fictional team in a Disney movie, are for real and Tuesday night they proved it, beating the Phoenix Coyotes 3-0 in the seventh game of their first-round series.
Now they face a real test - the formidable Detroit Red Wings, in the second round.
"Outside of the team's opening game (in 1993), this is the biggest night in Mighty Ducks history," club spokesman Bill Robertson said.
"This is no longer a movie. This is no longer a marketing device," wrote Los Angeles Times sports columnist Bill Plaschke. "This is real hockey."
The team boasts one of the most deadly twin offensive threats in the league - "Finnish Flash" Teemu Selanne and scoring sensation Paul Kariya.
Selanne, with 51 goals and 58 assists, and Kariya, with 44 goals and 55 assists, finished second and third in the overall league scoring table behind NHL legend Mario Lemieux.

Bouncing back from their worst start in the club's brief existence -- only one win and two ties in 12 games in October -- the Ducks ended the regular season behind only the defending Stanley Cup champion Colorado Avalanche in the Pacific Division. Their 85 points in the 82-game season made them fourth seeds in the Western Division playoffs.
For Walt Disney Co., which owns the Ducks, the team's success is another step on the road to building a sports annex to its global entertainment empire.

"Our extended goal all along has been to be competitive and make the playoffs," said Robertson, spokesman for the Ducks but also Disney Sports Enterprises. "We still have a long way to go, we haven't won a trophy yet, but this (Ducks' success) solidifies us (Disney) as major players."
The key to the success, he said, is marketing -- something Disney has plenty of experience doing, through its films, cartoons, theme parks and stores.

The Ducks' logo, for example, has been the top seller in NHL merchandise for four years, and is third in overall professional sports behind only basketball's Chicago Bulls and football's Dallas Cowboys.
"We view sports as an entertainment vehicle and players as performers," Robertson said, explaining Disney's philosophy toward sports.

Success on the ice "gives us brand identity. It drives a lot of things, like future season-ticket sales, sponsors and merchandise," said Robertson. "It is important to have continued success - it is one of the building blocks for Disney growth."

In addition to the Mighty Ducks, the company owns 25 percent of the Anaheim (formerly California) Angels of Major League Baseball and Robertson said the company is "looking to expand in other pro sports."

There has been speculation Disney might try to lure the National Basketball Association's Los Angeles Clippers 30 miles (50 km) south to Anaheim. But Robertson had no further comment on future Disney acquisitions.

The success of the Ducks -- who consistently sells out their 17,000-plus arena -- is also the story of the NHL's efforts to expand into the so-called Sun Belt, away from traditional hockey-playing Canadian and northeast U.S. cities.
The game's greatest player Wayne Gretzky had a lot to do with the sport's increased visibility when he took the Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup final.

Another expansion team, the Florida Panthers, who play in semi-tropical Miami, made it to the 1996 Stanley Cup finals, while the San Jose Sharks, Dallas Stars and Tampa Bay Lightning all draw good crowds in their sunny homes.
"The success of teams in the Sun Belt has spurred interest in cities where you wouldn't expect traditional interest in hockey," said the NHL's chief spokesman Arthur Pincus.

The league is currently considering six cities for future expansion and two of them - Atlanta and Houston - are in the Sun Belt. The others are Minneapolis-St. Paul, Nashville, Oklahoma City and Columbus, Ohio.
